newsitem.title: USA: Clinton plan has expected swipes at Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plan has expected swipes at Wall Street.

text.p: As expected, President Bill Clinton's five-year budget plan contained a grab-bag of revenue raisers that would hit investors and corporations.
Many of the proposals, projected to raise $34.3 billion over five years, are identical to measures proposed in 1995 and rejected by Congress.
Among the most controversial items, the Clinton plan would require investors to calculate capital gains taxes based on the average acquisition cost of investments.
People who buy stock or mutual funds over time often buy shares at different prices.

When someone decides to sell a portion of their holdings, current tax allows the investor to designate which shares are being sold when calculating capital gains. That lets investors minimize their taxable gains by choosing to sell the shares that cost the most to acquire.

The provision to force investors to use the average cost whenever they sell a portion of their investments, projected to raise $3 billion over five years, has already drawn fire from the securities and mutual fund industries.
The proposal would apply to all stocks, notes, bonds and derivative instruments.
Clinton also proposed eliminating a popular strategy used to avoid capital gains taxes known as "shorting against the box."
Instead of selling stock, which would trigger capital gains taxes, an investor borrows the same shares from a brokerage firm and sells the borrowed stock.
The plan would raise $300 million over five years by triggering capital gains taxes when investors short against the box or use similiar strategies.

Clinton also proposed reducing the amount of dividends a corporation can receive tax-free to 50 percent from 70 percent, modifying the holding period for the tax break and disqualifying dividends from certain limited-term preferred stock. The measures would raise $3 billion.

The plan would also quash a host of popular capital raising strategies used by corporations that reduce tax receipts, including sales of bonds with maturities of more than 40 years, trust preferred stock and original issue discount convertible stock.
A favorite tax-free spin-off technique, known as a Morris Trust transaction, would also be eliminated under the Clinton plan, saving the Treasury a projected $300 million.

A company would no longer avoid paying capital gains taxes on a spin-off to a corporation under its control unless shareholders of the company retained at least a 50 percent ownership in both entities for two years before and two years after the transaction. Unrelated transactions such as public trading on the stock market would be disregarded.
Another $2.9 billion would be raised by limiting the use of net operating losses as tax write-offs in future years.

The single largest revenue raiser in the package, totaling $7.5 billion over five years, would change the rules for U.S. multinational exporters. The proposal reduces the amount of export sales income that such companies may treat as derived from foreign sources.
Also included in the total $34.3 billion is $6 billion of revenue related to changes in Federal Unemployment Act provisions and $1.1 billion from extending oil spill exicse taxes.
